note: Rule WEIGHTS are policy and are hand-authored here on purpose: they encode what a
review of each app is FOR, which is a decision, not a measurement.
STACK facts are the opposite and are deliberately ABSENT. PIPELINE_SPEC C11 bans
prose as a source for them, and its own worked example is a table that banned prose
and then published three unmeasured cells in the fix. `stack` is therefore null in
every profile below and is filled by a live `dr surface` read of the checkout. A
consumer that needs a framework version must read it from there and must fail rather
than default when it is null.

why: A purchased template. Its design system is not ours, so conformance to it is not
a defect we can act on -- a token-drift finding here resolves to 'the vendor chose
that', and a review that leads with forty of them buries the two findings a person
would act on. What DOES bind is anything a reader experiences: contrast, clipped
text, targets you cannot hit, and whether the page reads in the intended order.
So conformance is demoted, correctness is full weight, and the judgement classes
carry the review -- which is also the only app of the three where they should.
An internal dashboard on our own system. Here conformance IS the review: a card
with the wrong radius or a label off the scale is a real, actionable, cheap fix,
and the deterministic layer finds all of it with no model call. The judgement
classes shrink to the two a dashboard actually fails at -- a table that does not
fit its data, and a label that promises something the rows do not do (both were
found by the blind reviewer on this corpus and by no rule).
Its `type-scale` rule will abstain, not fail, wherever no token map declares a
scale. An engine with no declared scale cannot produce a conformance verdict, and
a confident FAIL whose truth depends on which resolver ran is worse than silence.
Between the two, and the weights say so rather than picking a side. Its class
names are runtime hashes, so a conformance finding here is often unattributable
to a source line even when it is correct -- which is a reason to rank it below a
correctness finding, not a reason to stop computing it.
The corpus's own profile: everything at 1.0, nothing demoted. The bench exists to
measure the detectors, and a weighting is exactly the thing that would stop it.
